title: Catch-up and revision: lessons 12 to 16
footer: 1.2 Lesson 16: Catch-up and revision: lessons 12 to 16
starter: Without notes, write the three file size formulas: images, sound and text.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Character sets
facts: A character set links characters to binary codes.
ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters. Unicode: 16+ bits, every writing system.
stations.challenge: Explain why Unicode files are larger than ASCII files.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A character set links characters to binary codes.
Also credit: ASCII: 7 bits, 128 characters. Unicode: 16+ bits, every writing system.

questions.q: How many characters can 8 bits represent?
What is the advantage of Unicode?
questions.a: It can represent characters from every writing system

questions.q: A text file has 100 characters in 8-bit ASCII. How big is it?

stations.name: Images
facts: File size = width × height × colour depth.
Colour depth is bits per pixel; n bits give 2ⁿ colours.
Metadata stores dimensions, colour depth, date and more.
stations.challenge: Calculate the size of a 500 × 500 image at 8-bit colour depth.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: File size = width × height × colour depth.
Also credit: Colour depth is bits per pixel; n bits give 2ⁿ colours.

questions.q: What is the formula for an image's file size?
A colour depth of 4 bits gives how many colours?
Which is an example of metadata?
questions.a: The date the image was taken

stations.name: Sound
facts: File size = sample rate × bit depth × duration.
Sample rate is samples per second; bit depth is bits per sample.
Higher values mean better quality and bigger files.
stations.challenge: Calculate the size of 20 seconds at 16,000 Hz and 8-bit depth.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: File size = sample rate × bit depth × duration.
Also credit: Sample rate is samples per second; bit depth is bits per sample.

questions.q: What does bit depth mean for sound?
questions.a: The number of bits used to store each sample

questions.q: Doubling the sample rate does what to the file?
questions.a: Doubles its size and improves quality

questions.q: What is sampling?
questions.a: Measuring the wave's amplitude at regular intervals

stations.name: Compression
facts: Lossy: data removed permanently, much smaller files, used for photos, music and video.
Lossless: nothing lost, the original can be restored, used for text and programs.
Run-length encoding is a lossless method.
stations.challenge: State two reasons why data is compressed.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Lossy: data removed permanently, much smaller files, used for photos, music and video.
Also credit: Lossless: nothing lost, the original can be restored, used for text and programs.

questions.q: Which type of compression is used for MP3 files?
Why can't a program file use lossy compression?
questions.a: Missing data would stop the program working

questions.q: How does run-length encoding save space?
questions.a: It stores a colour once with the number of times it repeats

stations.name: Calculations practice
facts: Write the formula, substitute the numbers, then convert the units.
Divide bits by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kB and again for MB.
stations.challenge: Complete the three calculations on your worksheet.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Write the formula, substitute the numbers, then convert the units.
Also credit: Divide bits by 8 for bytes, then by 1,000 for kB and again for MB.

questions.q: A 400 × 300 image has 8-bit colour. What is the size in kB?
A 60-second sound is 22,050 Hz at 16 bits. Roughly how large is it?
A 2,000-character file uses 16-bit Unicode. How big is it in bytes?

stations.name: Exam technique
facts: Show your working: method marks are available even if the final number is wrong.
Watch the units the question asks for.
Learn the definitions: sampling, metadata, character set, lossy, lossless.
stations.challenge: Which command words appear most in this topic?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Show your working: method marks are available even if the final number is wrong.
Also credit: Watch the units the question asks for.

questions.q: A question says 'calculate' and is worth 3 marks. What should you include?
questions.a: The formula, the substituted numbers and the final answer with units

questions.q: A question asks for the answer in kilobytes but you have bits. What do you do?
Which definition is correct?
questions.a: Metadata is data about the data, such as an image's dimensions

final.name: Final challenge: data representation

questions.q: Convert the character code 90 (the letter Z) into 8-bit binary.
Which part of the topic does each fact belong to?
questions.a: ASCII uses 7 bits per character = Text; Colour depth is bits per pixel = Images; Sample rate is measured in hertz = Sound; Lossy removes data permanently = Compression; Metadata stores the dimensions = Images; Unicode covers every writing system = Text; Bit depth sets the number of levels = Sound; Run-length encoding is lossless = Compression

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
points: Learn the definitions: sampling, metadata, character set, lossy, lossless.
Run-length encoding is a lossless method.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 4.

exam.q: An image is 640 × 480 with 8-bit colour depth. Calculate its size in kilobytes.
points: File size = width × height × colour depth.
Colour depth is bits per pixel; n bits give 2ⁿ colours.
Metadata stores dimensions, colour depth, date and more.
File size = sample rate × bit depth × duration.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
